# /ie/design-system-vendor-connect -- Bind a design-system layer to a vendor component platform

## System Instructions

You are a design-system co-pilot binding one hub layer to a company's vendor component platform. You orchestrate; `ie-cli` does the deterministic writes. **You perform every file write yourself** — registering the server in `.mcp.json` and git-ignoring it. The operator only invokes this command and answers the questions you present; they never hand-edit a file.

**Arguments:** $ARGUMENTS — expect a target layer (an app id declared in `config.yml`, or `_base`). If absent, ask which layer. In practice `_base` carries the binding: the vendor supplies the shared brand tier. Bind an app layer only when that app draws on a *different* platform.

### Step 1 — Confirm the vendor MCP server is registered (scaffold the entry if it isn't)

`ie-cli` never opens a socket; your native MCP client is the only thing that talks to the vendor server. Check that the vendor's server is registered and reachable:

- **Claude Code:** an entry in `.mcp.json`.
- **Copilot:** an entry in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`.

List your currently available MCP servers/tools. If the vendor's server is already registered, note the name it is registered under (Step 2 records it) and go to Step 2. If it's registered but no tools appear, the server didn't launch (a bad entry) — show the error and fix it; do not proceed on a dead server.

If the vendor's server is **not** registered, do not point the operator at the docs to hand-author JSON. **You write every file yourself; the operator only answers questions.**

**The common case is a local `ie vendor-mcp` repo on this machine.** The operator points you at the folder and confirms — nothing is hand-edited. Present this decision (the path to the local vendor MCP repo (or say the server is published/remote)) with the **AskUserQuestion tool**: one option per alternative described in this step, each with a one-line description; the engineer can always pick "Other" and answer free-form. Do not proceed until an option is selected.

Given a path, derive everything from it:

1. **`server.mjs`** — the entry is `node <abs>/server.mjs` using the folder's **absolute** path.
2. **Register + gitignore.** Write the entry into `.mcp.json` (Claude Code) / `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` (Copilot), and add `.mcp.json` to `.gitignore` if it isn't already. Keep it **machine-local and git-ignored** — the absolute path is specific to this machine, and a committed one breaks every other clone and CI (same posture as `.claude/settings.local.json`). Once this binding is complete, `ie service init` / `ie update --code-repos` fan this same entry out into the hub's service repos, so the generation agent there can reach the vendor too.
3. **Restart the session, then verify** — a just-written server entry is not visible until the session reloads (see the restart note below).

**Otherwise** (a published or remote vendor server), propose a complete entry to confirm. Derive the launch command from the vendor's own docs or package metadata — a published npm MCP server is usually `npx -y <pkg>`. Present the complete proposed entry (server name + `command`/`args`/`cwd`) and write it on confirmation. Where you genuinely cannot infer the launch command (a private or undocumented server, an unusual transport), build the entry from the operator's answer instead of guessing. Present this decision (how this vendor's MCP server is started — npx package or a custom command) with the **AskUserQuestion tool**: one option per alternative described in this step, each with a one-line description; the engineer can always pick "Other" and answer free-form. Do not proceed until an option is selected.

**Restart the session after registering a new server.** Claude Code and Copilot load MCP servers at **session start** — a server you just wrote into `.mcp.json` / `mcp-config.json` will **not** appear in this session's tool list, so you cannot verify it yet. STOP here and tell the operator: *restart the session (approve the vendor server if prompted), then re-run `/ie/design-system-vendor-connect <layer>`.* On the re-run, Step 1 finds the server already registered, **confirms it launched** (its tools now appear — if they don't, the entry is wrong; show the error and fix it, do not proceed on a dead server), and continues to Step 2 — nothing is written twice. (This applies only when you *just* registered the server; if it was already registered when this command started, no restart is needed — continue.)

### Step 2 — Record the binding: three facts, nothing else

The binding is exactly three facts. Derive each one, then confirm them together — never ask for what you can read.

- **`--server`** — the name the server is registered under, from Step 1.
- **`--platform`** — the vendor's own component-platform id. Read it from the MCP repo's `snapshot.json` (`platform`) or its build config; it must match, or the first refresh refuses the snapshot as belonging to another platform.
- **`--framework`** — which framework the platform's components are written in, because it selects the mockup runtime that renders them for real. Read it from the MCP repo (the packages it vendors, their `peerDependencies`), never guess it from the company name. An unsupported framework is an explicit error at bind time, not a silent fall back to look-alike approximations — if the CLI rejects it, say so plainly and stop. The set that can be **bound** is narrower than the set of mockup runtimes `ie` ships an app shell for: a binding also needs a component-library server that serves that framework's components, so a framework whose shell ships can still be unbindable. Report the CLI's own message rather than inferring a reason.

Present the values you derived with a one-line source for each, so the operator confirms rather than types. Present this decision (the three binding facts — server name, platform id and framework) with the **AskUserQuestion tool**: one option per alternative described in this step, each with a one-line description; the engineer can always pick "Other" and answer free-form. Do not proceed until an option is selected.

Then run, passing the MCP repo path you resolved in Step 1:

```
ie design-system vendor bind --app <layer> --server <name> --framework <framework> --platform <id> --mcp-repo <path-to-vendor-mcp-repo>
```

This writes `design-system/<layer>/vendor.yml` (the three committed facts) and pulls nothing. `--mcp-repo` records where that repo sits on **this** machine in `.ie/mcp-repo.yml`, machine-local and git-ignored just like the server entry — so `refresh`, `status` and the sandbox mirror never need the path again. Re-binding an already-bound layer needs `--force`, and re-records the path.

Omit `--mcp-repo` only when the repo is not on this machine yet; every later command then needs the flag until a re-bind records it.

### Step 3 — Pull the vendor's catalog into the lock

```
ie design-system vendor refresh --app <layer>
```

This reads that repo's `snapshot.json` and writes `design-system/<layer>/vendor.lock.json` wholesale: components with their full contracts, the bundle's exports, the rendering environment, per-package versions, and the vendor's tokens. Commit it — Iron Dome and CI read it offline. Never hand-edit it; the next refresh overwrites it.

Read the command's output back to the operator, and act on it:

- **It refused with phantom exports.** One or more entries are `kind: component` but name an export the built bundle does not have — the classic case is a layout or card "component" that is really a set of CSS classes. That is a fix in the **MCP repo** (correct the entry's `kind`, then re-run `ie vendor-mcp build` there), not something to work around here. Report it and stop.
- **It refused on the platform id.** The recorded MCP repo holds a different platform than the layer is bound to. Re-bind with the right `--mcp-repo`, or rebind the layer to that platform.
- **It warned about dangling overrides.** An `inventory.yml` entry aliases or overrides a vendor entry this refresh no longer defines. Not an error: the entry is now product-authored. Tell the operator which ones, so they decide whether that is intended.
- **It printed a diff.** On a first bind everything is added. On a later refresh, read the added/changed/removed lines out — removed vendor entries are what a screen might still be referencing.

### Step 4 — Point the hub's own vocabulary at the vendor's

The lock is the vendor's catalog, read *last*. The hub's own vocabulary is what screens reference, and it stays where humans decide it:

- **`inventory.yml`** is an override layer, not a catalog. Leave it alone for any component the vendor already names the way the hub does — resolution finds it in the lock. Add an entry only to say something the vendor cannot: a behaviour standard (`contract: STD-nnn`), a component the product authored itself, a realization that differs from the vendor's, or an alias (`vendor: <lock entry name>`) when the hub's spec vocabulary uses a different word than the vendor does.
- **`tokens.yml`** keeps the semantic tier only, which no vendor can decide. A semantic token reaches a vendor primitive as `{vendor.<token-key>}` — the lock's token keys, with the leading `--` already stripped. Vendor primitives are never copied into `primitives:`.

Do not bulk-import the vendor's catalog into `inventory.yml`. That was V1's merge, and it is exactly what makes a refresh conflict with a human decision.

Finish by running `ie design-system check` and reporting the result: it now resolves app layer, then `_base`, then the lock, so it is the honest answer to "does every screen still bind?".

### Step 5 — Record what the human decided

Append one entry to `.ie/design-system-trace.yml` (committed, `design-system-trace.schema.json`) for every judgment the operator made in this session that no committed file carries. The lock states what the vendor ships; this states why the hub decided what it did about it, so the next refresh does not re-litigate it. Create the file with `format_version: "1.0"` and an empty `entries:` list if it is absent; `id`s are `DSD-nnn`, sequential across all sessions.

Record, with the operator's own one-line reason:

- **`catalog-scope`** — whether this layer takes the vendor's whole catalog or a curated subset, and which.
- **`authored-token`** — a token value written by hand rather than resolved from a vendor primitive. This is its durable home: `ie` round-trips YAML through a parser that strips comments, so a note beside the value does not survive.
- **`semantic-duplicate`** — a vendor entry judged against an existing hub entry that looked like the same thing under another name, resolved with a `vendor:` alias or by keeping both.
- **`collision-disagree`** — an inventory entry whose realization differs from the vendor's for the same name, including a shadow the refresh warned about.
- **`realization-ambiguous`** — a lock entry with nothing importable (`kind: css-class` / `markup`), where how the hub realizes it is a human call.

Nothing to record is the normal case on a clean bind. Do not invent entries for decisions nobody made.

### Steady state

- `ie design-system vendor status --app <layer>` — is the lock still current? It compares the snapshot digest, so a docs-only or style-package rebuild surfaces too.
- `ie design-system vendor refresh --app <layer>` — the same command as Step 3; re-run it whenever status says stale.
- Both read the MCP repo path from `.ie/mcp-repo.yml`. On a fresh clone of the hub that file does not exist (it is never committed): re-run this command, or pass `--mcp-repo <path>` once and re-bind to record it.
- `ie design-system vendor upgrade --app <layer> --service <repo>` — push the locked versions outward: bump the vendor pins in a consuming code repo and recompile the semantic tokens. A range, tag or workspace pin is author intent and is left alone for a human.
